title: Education
author: Lyon, G. Reid
summary: G. Reid Lyon, Ph.D., former chief of the Child Development and Behavior Branch at NICHD, makes the case that the science of reading is trustworthy not because any single study has settled the question but because of the cumulative, self-correcting, multi-disciplinary convergence of evidence built over more than six decades. The article distinguishes principled scientific knowledge tested across cognitive psychology, developmental psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, and genetics from the advocacy positions and pedagogical fashion cycles that have dominated reading instruction policy. Lyon acknowledges the science is often weaponized by advocates and distorted by political interests, but argues this distortion is a feature of the communication environment, not a flaw in the underlying evidence. The essay credits Emily Hanford's Sold a Story series with translating the evidence base into public terms that moved policy, while noting the evidence had been established long before the public narrative shifted. Lyon's closing concern is forward-looking: even as states adopt reading science in policy, the persistent pattern of failed institutionalization suggests implementation will be contested unless structural barriers in teacher prep and curriculum adoption are directly confronted.
points: The credibility of the science of reading rests on convergent replication across six decades of independent research spanning cognitive psychology, neuroscience, genetics, linguistics, and developmental psychology, a cross-disciplinary consensus extremely rare in educational research.

Lyon distinguishes the evidence base from the advocacy: the science of reading is reliable; the communication, institutionalization, and application of that science has been persistently and damagingly poor, a different problem requiring different solutions.

The most significant barrier to applying reading science is not ignorance but institutional inertia: teacher preparation programs, curriculum publishers, and assessment systems built around non-scientific frameworks whose economic interests align with resisting change.

Emily Hanford's Sold a Story was effective not because it discovered new evidence but because it translated decades-old established evidence into narrative form that public audiences and policymakers could act on.

Even as states adopt reading science in policy, the persistent pattern of failed institutionalization across prior cycles means implementation will be contested unless structural barriers in teacher prep, curriculum adoption, and assessment are directly confronted.
quotes: I am honored to share an article by Reid Lyon titled "Why We Can Trust the Science of Reading." Reid and I have been colleagues for nearly 40 years, during which I have observed his leadership in orchestrating the NICHD literacy research program and his multifaceted dissemination efforts.

Although many other researchers have contributed to our understanding of how people learn to read, without the NICHD convergent findings, Emily Hanford's Sold a Story series would have been hard-pressed to have had such a strong impact on the public and on state policy regarding the legitimacy of requiring that evidence be used to teach reading, developmentally and remedially.

Reid concludes by highlighting "...the persistent failure to communicate, translate, institutionalize, and sustain the application of knowledge that has already demonstrated its validity and durability." Reid and I discuss how to address this failure in our recent podcast "Building Our Profession..." I delve deeply into the challenge of building our profession in "What Education Can Learn from Trusted Professions." Why We Can Trust the Science of Reading" Page 1
